domain: Developing Code for Data Processing using Python and SQL

questions.q: A team writes a Python UDF to upper-case a column in a nightly ETL job over billions of rows. What does Databricks recommend instead?

options.t: Use the built-in function, because built-in Spark functions are optimized for distributed processing
Move it to a Scala UDF, which Databricks recommends for every regular ETL workload
options.why: Scala UDFs are faster than Python ones, but a built-in function needs no UDF at all.

options.t: Wrap it in a pandas UDF and leave everything else as it is, since UDFs suit large ETL
options.why: Databricks recommends UDFs for ad hoc and small-to-medium work, and Spark methods for large regular ETL.

options.t: Rewrite it as a session-scoped Python UDF registered once at the start of each job run, so it is compiled only once
options.why: Still a Python UDF: data still leaves the JVM row by row.

questions.explain: Databricks recommends UDFs for logic that's hard to express with built-in functions, and built-in Spark functions for large datasets and workloads that run regularly, because they are optimized for distributed processing.

questions.q: Why are pandas UDFs typically much faster than row-at-a-time Python UDFs?

options.t: They are compiled to Scala bytecode when the job starts
options.why: Nothing is compiled to Scala; they run in Python with pandas.

options.t: They use Apache Arrow to move data in batches, reducing serialization costs
They skip the shuffle entirely, whatever the query does
options.why: A UDF doesn't change the query's shuffles.

options.t: They run inside the JVM next to the executors, so no data ever has to be handed to a Python process
options.why: pandas UDFs still run in Python; Arrow makes the transfer cheap.

questions.explain: The UDF page: pandas UDFs are up to 100x faster than Python UDFs because they use Apache Arrow to reduce serialization costs, working on batches with vectorized pandas operations.

questions.q: A pandas UDF must load a machine-learning model file once and apply it to every batch of rows. Which pandas UDF type fits?

options.t: Series to Series, loading the model inside the function body for each batch
options.why: That would reload the model for every batch.

options.t: A row-at-a-time Python UDF that caches the model in a global variable on the driver
options.why: A driver global doesn't reach the Python workers that run the UDF, and row-at-a-time UDFs are the slow kind.

options.t: Iterator of Series to Iterator of Series
Series to scalar, used through groupBy().agg()
options.why: That aggregates a group to one value; it doesn't keep state across batches.

questions.explain: The iterator variant receives an iterator of batches, so state such as a loaded model is initialised once and applied to every input batch: the pandas UDF page's own example.

questions.q: A Series to scalar pandas UDF is used in groupBy().agg() over a few very large groups, and executors run out of memory. What explains it?

options.t: Arrow batches are capped at 10,000 rows, so each large group is split across several executors and reassembled
options.why: The batch size controls transfer, not how groups are aggregated.

options.t: The UDF's type hint is wrong, so Spark falls back to row-at-a-time processing
options.why: A wrong hint gives an error or another UDF type, not this memory behaviour.

options.t: Series to scalar UDFs always run on the driver, never on executors
options.why: They run on executors like other UDFs.

options.t: This UDF type doesn't support partial aggregation, so all of a group's data is loaded into memory

questions.explain: The pandas UDF page says Series to scalar UDFs do not support partial aggregation: all data for each group is loaded into memory, so very large groups can exhaust it.

questions.q: An analyst can see the function `finance.tools.mask_iban` in Catalog Explorer but gets a permission error when calling it. Which privilege on the function is missing?

options.t: EXECUTE
SELECT
options.why: SELECT applies to tables and views.

options.t: MODIFY on the function
options.why: MODIFY is for changing table data.

options.t: BROWSE
options.why: BROWSE lets people see that objects exist, which they already can.

questions.explain: Running a Unity Catalog function needs EXECUTE on it, with the usage privileges on its schema and catalog: `GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION finance.tools.mask_iban TO ...`.

questions.q: How is a Python function registered in Unity Catalog so other teams can call it from SQL?

options.t: `spark.udf.register('fn', f)` in a notebook, which persists it to the current schema
options.why: That registers a session-scoped UDF that exists only in the SparkSession.

options.t: `CREATE FUNCTION cat.sch.fn(...) RETURNS ... LANGUAGE PYTHON AS $$ ... $$`
Uploading the .py file to a volume, which publishes every function in it
options.why: A volume stores files; it doesn't register functions.

options.t: `ALTER SCHEMA cat.sch ADD FUNCTION fn` followed by a cluster restart
options.why: There is no such statement.

questions.explain: Unity Catalog functions are created with CREATE FUNCTION named catalog.schema.function; Python bodies sit between $$ delimiters. They are governed, discoverable and reusable across sessions.

questions.q: A view calls a Unity Catalog Python function. On which compute does querying the view fail?

options.t: A serverless SQL warehouse, because serverless can't run Python
options.why: Serverless and pro SQL warehouses support Python in UC functions.

options.t: A pro SQL warehouse, because it runs only SQL functions
options.why: Pro SQL warehouses are listed as supported.

options.t: A classic SQL warehouse
A cluster on Databricks Runtime 13.3 LTS in standard access mode
options.why: DBR 13.3 LTS and above is supported.

questions.explain: The UC functions page: Python code in UC functions needs a serverless or pro SQL warehouse or DBR 13.3 LTS+, and a view that includes a UC Python UDF fails on classic SQL warehouses.

questions.q: Which statement about session-scoped and Unity Catalog governed UDFs is correct?

options.t: A session-scoped UDF is shared with every notebook attached to the same cluster for as long as the cluster runs
options.why: It is scoped to the current SparkSession only.

options.t: Governed UDFs exist only for SQL; Python logic can only ever be session-scoped
options.why: Governed UDFs can be written in SQL, Python, Scala and Java.

options.t: Both kinds are listed in Catalog Explorer, but only governed ones accept arguments
options.why: Session-scoped UDFs aren't governed or discoverable there.

options.t: A session-scoped UDF exists only in the current SparkSession; a governed one is persisted and reusable

questions.explain: Governed UDFs are persisted in Unity Catalog, controlled by its permissions and discoverable in Catalog Explorer; session-scoped ones exist only for the current session.

questions.q: Salaries in a department are 21000, 23000, 23000 and 29000, ordered ascending. What does RANK() give them?

options.why: That ignores the tie.
That is DENSE_RANK.
Only the two 23000 salaries tie.

questions.explain: RANK gives tied rows the same rank and leaves a gap after them (1, 2, 2, 4); DENSE_RANK leaves no gap (1, 2, 2, 3). Both appear in the window functions page's examples.

questions.q: A query uses `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`. Why is it rejected?

options.t: ROW_NUMBER needs a PARTITION BY clause in every window, and this one has none
options.why: Without PARTITION BY the partition is simply all rows.

options.t: A ranking function's window must have ORDER BY and no frame clause
Frames are allowed only with RANGE, never with ROWS
options.why: Both ROWS and RANGE frames exist.

options.t: ORDER BY isn't allowed in an OVER clause, only in the outer query
options.why: ORDER BY orders rows within the window.

questions.explain: The window functions page: for a ranking function, the window specification must include an ORDER BY clause, but not a window frame clause.

questions.q: Each customer's events are in a table. You need, on every row, the previous event's timestamp for the same customer. Which expression fits?

options.t: `MAX(ts) OVER (ORDER BY customer_id)` over the whole table without partitions
options.why: That is a running maximum across customers, not the previous event.

options.t: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) - 1` joined back to the table on the result
options.why: That numbers rows; it isn't a timestamp, and without ORDER BY it is rejected.

options.t: `LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ts)`
`LEAD(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ts)`
options.why: LEAD returns the next row's value.

questions.explain: LAG and LEAD are analytic window functions: LAG reads the previous row in the window's order, LEAD the next. PARTITION BY restarts the window for each customer.

questions.q: A window has no PARTITION BY clause. What does each row's window cover?

options.t: An error is raised, because PARTITION BY is required
options.why: PARTITION BY is optional.

options.t: Only the current row, so the function returns the row's own value
options.why: Without partitions the window isn't limited to one row.

options.t: The rows of the current task's partition on the executor, so results depend on how the data was split
options.why: SQL partitions aren't the same as Spark task partitions.

options.t: All rows of the query result, ordered by the ORDER BY clause if one is given

questions.explain: The page: if no PARTITION clause is specified, the partition is comprised of all rows.

questions.q: JSON payloads arrive as strings and their structure changes often. What does Databricks recommend storing them as?

options.t: VARIANT, created with parse_json
STRING, parsed with from_json in every query
options.why: Databricks recommends VARIANT over JSON strings.

options.t: BINARY, so nothing is lost
options.why: BINARY can't be queried by path.

options.t: A STRUCT inferred from the first file and never changed
options.why: A fixed struct breaks when the structure changes.

questions.explain: The VARIANT page: Databricks recommends VARIANT over JSON strings for semi-structured data; create values with parse_json.

questions.q: `variant_get(raw, '$.price', 'int')` runs on a row where price is the string "cheap". What happens?

options.t: It returns 0, the default for INT
options.why: There is no default value.

options.t: It fails with INVALID_VARIANT_CAST; try_variant_get would return NULL instead
It returns the string unchanged, because a VARIANT always keeps each value's original type
options.why: The requested type is INT, so the value is cast or fails.

options.t: It returns NULL, as it does for a missing path
options.why: NULL is returned for a missing path; a failed cast is an error.

questions.explain: variant_get returns NULL when the path is missing and raises INVALID_VARIANT_CAST when the value can't be cast to the type; try_variant_get returns NULL instead of the error.

questions.q: A table has a VARIANT column `raw`. Which statement is allowed?

options.t: `SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY raw`
options.why: VARIANT can't be used for ordering.

options.t: `ALTER TABLE t CLUSTER BY (raw)`
options.why: VARIANT columns can't be clustering keys.

options.t: `SELECT raw:customer.id::STRING FROM t`
`SELECT raw, count(*) FROM t GROUP BY raw`
options.why: VARIANT can't be used for grouping.

questions.explain: Use `:` for a top-level field, `.` for nested ones and `::` to cast. VARIANT can't be a clustering, partition or Z-order key, and can't be used for comparisons, grouping, ordering or set operations.

questions.q: A payload has a top-level field `Owner`. A query reads `raw:owner`. What does it return?

options.t: The Owner value, because VARIANT paths ignore the case of field names
options.why: Field names are always case sensitive.

options.t: An error, because a field must be read with variant_get
options.why: The `:` path syntax is valid.

options.t: The whole payload, because the path didn't match
options.why: A missing path gives NULL.

options.t: NULL, because field names in VARIANT paths are case sensitive

questions.explain: VARIANT field names are always case sensitive, and a path that isn't found returns NULL.

questions.q: A team wants to call `ai_query` from Databricks SQL. Which compute can't run it?

options.t: A classic SQL warehouse
A serverless SQL warehouse
options.why: Serverless SQL warehouses can run AI Functions.

options.t: A pro SQL warehouse
options.why: Only classic SQL warehouses are excluded.

options.t: A notebook on a cluster with Databricks Runtime 15.4 LTS
options.why: DBR 15.4 LTS or above is required, which this meets.

questions.explain: AI Functions, ai_query included, are not available on classic SQL warehouses, and need DBR 15.4 LTS or above on clusters.

questions.q: A batch job runs ai_query over 2 million rows. Some rows produce bad responses, and the team wants those rows flagged rather than failing the query. What do they set?

options.t: Split the table into 1,000-row slices and run ai_query on each slice in a loop, retrying the failures
options.why: Databricks advises one query over the full dataset rather than manual batches.

options.t: `failOnError => false`, so ai_query returns a struct with the response and an error message
`returnType => 'STRING'`, which converts errors to empty strings
options.why: returnType sets the type of the parsed response.

options.t: `modelParameters => named_struct('temperature', 0.0)`
options.why: Temperature changes the model's output, not error handling.

questions.explain: failOnError defaults to true. Set to false, ai_query returns a struct with the parsed response and an error message per row. Databricks also advises submitting the full dataset in a single query.

questions.q: What does `ai_query` do?

options.t: Rewrites a SQL query in natural language for documentation
options.why: It sends a request to a model endpoint.

options.t: Searches the workspace's notebooks for an answer to a question
options.why: It queries a serving endpoint.

options.t: Calls an existing Databricks Model Serving endpoint and parses its response
Trains a new model on the query's result and registers it in Unity Catalog for later use
options.why: It invokes an endpoint; it doesn't train.

questions.explain: ai_query invokes an existing Model Serving endpoint (Foundation Model, external or custom) and is billed for that endpoint; task-specific functions such as ai_classify or ai_summarize cover common tasks.

questions.q: A streaming job is scheduled every hour to process everything that arrived since the last run, then stop. Which trigger fits?

options.t: `.trigger(continuous='1 second')`
options.why: Continuous processing isn't supported on Databricks.

options.t: `.trigger(once=True)`, which Databricks recommends for new code
options.why: Trigger.Once is deprecated since DBR 11.3 LTS; availableNow replaces it.

options.t: `.trigger(processingTime='1 hour')` in a continuous job that never stops
options.why: That keeps the query running between batches.

options.t: `.trigger(availableNow=True)`

questions.explain: availableNow processes everything available and stops: incremental batch for scheduled jobs. It is also what serverless notebooks and jobs support.

questions.q: Two streaming queries are given the same checkpointLocation. What is the rule?

options.t: Each query needs its own checkpoint location; never share one
The second query automatically gets a sub-folder of the first's checkpoint
options.why: Nothing is created automatically.

options.t: It works if they read different topics
options.why: Each query needs its own checkpoint, whatever it reads.

options.t: It is recommended to save storage
options.why: Never share a checkpoint.

questions.explain: A checkpoint stores one query's offsets, commits, state and query ID. Each query needs its own location; sharing one fails (DELTA_CONCURRENT_TRANSACTION, §24).

questions.q: A running aggregation needs a new stateful operation added. What does the checkpoint guidance say?

options.t: It is always safe across restarts, like adding a filter or changing the trigger interval
options.why: Changing stateful operations generally needs a new checkpoint.

options.t: Changing the stateful operations generally needs a new checkpoint
The checkpoint is upgraded automatically on restart
options.why: Nothing upgrades it automatically.

options.t: Only the trigger interval must change to match
options.why: Trigger intervals are safe to change, but that isn't the issue here.

questions.explain: Changes to sources, stateful operation types, state schema or sink type generally need a new checkpoint; filters, rate limits and trigger intervals are generally safe.

questions.q: A windowed count uses `withWatermark('event_time', '10 minutes')`. What does the watermark do?

options.t: It delays every result by exactly 10 minutes of wall-clock time, whatever the event times are
options.why: It bounds lateness by event time; it isn't a delay.

options.t: Drops records whose processing takes more than 10 minutes
options.why: It concerns event time, not processing time.

options.t: Bounds the state kept: state older than the threshold is dropped, and later records may be ignored
Guarantees records up to 10 hours late are included
options.why: Only lateness within the threshold is guaranteed.

questions.explain: The engine tracks the latest event time and drops state older than the threshold. Records within the threshold are always processed; later ones might not be.

questions.q: A stream must MERGE each micro-batch into a Delta table. Which API is used?

options.t: `writeStream.format('delta').option('merge', 'true')`, keyed on the table's primary key
options.why: There is no merge option on the Delta sink.

options.t: `writeStream.outputMode('update')` alone, which merges by key
options.why: Update mode emits changed rows; it doesn't MERGE.

options.t: `writeStream.foreach(fn)` with one MERGE per row
options.why: Per-row MERGE isn't the documented pattern; foreachBatch is.

options.t: `writeStream.foreachBatch(fn)`, with fn running the MERGE on each batch

questions.explain: foreachBatch runs batch code on each micro-batch and is required for Delta MERGE from a stream. It gives at-least-once writes, so use batch_id to make them idempotent.

questions.q: A foreachBatch function appends each batch to an external table. After a restart, one batch is written twice. Why?

options.t: foreachBatch gives at-least-once writes; use batch_id to make them idempotent
The checkpoint was in the default location, which is cleared each time the job restarts
options.why: Every query must set a checkpoint; that isn't the cause.

options.t: Appends are not allowed in foreachBatch
options.why: Any batch write is allowed.

options.t: foreachBatch is exactly-once, so this must be a bug in the sink
options.why: foreachBatch gives at-least-once.

questions.explain: A batch can run again after a failure, so foreachBatch writes are at-least-once. Recording batch_id with the output (or MERGE on a key) makes a repeat harmless.

questions.q: A streaming aggregation without a watermark uses output mode `complete`. What is the documented drawback?

options.t: It drops old state as soon as the watermark passes, so late updates are lost
options.why: Complete mode never drops state.

options.t: It rewrites the whole result each trigger and scales poorly
It emits only rows that will never change
options.why: That is append mode.

options.t: It can't be used with aggregations
options.why: Complete mode is for aggregations only.

questions.explain: Complete mode rewrites the whole result every trigger and never drops state; Databricks suggests materialized views instead for that need.

questions.q: A serverless job runs a stream with `.trigger(processingTime='30 seconds')`. What happens?

options.t: It runs once and then waits for the next schedule
options.why: Processing-time triggers aren't supported there.

options.t: It runs as configured, starting a new micro-batch every 30 seconds until the job is stopped
options.why: Serverless jobs support only AvailableNow and Once.

options.t: It isn't supported: serverless notebooks and jobs support only AvailableNow (and Once)
It is silently converted to continuous processing
options.why: Continuous isn't supported on Databricks.

questions.explain: Serverless notebooks and jobs support only AvailableNow and Once triggers; time-based trigger intervals need classic compute.

questions.q: When does Databricks' guidance favour a declarative pipeline over hand-written Structured Streaming plus jobs?

options.t: Only when the source is a Kafka topic
options.why: Pipelines handle many sources.

options.t: Never: pipelines are for batch only
options.why: Pipelines handle batch and streaming.

options.t: When you need low-level control of every micro-batch and every sink API the job writes to
options.why: That is what hand-written Structured Streaming is for.

options.t: When you want orchestration, retries, data quality and incremental refresh handled for you

questions.explain: Lakeflow pipelines run flows in dependency order, retry transient failures, check expectations and refresh incrementally; Structured Streaming is the most customisable layer underneath.

questions.q: A CDC feed of customer changes, possibly out of order, must keep the full history of each customer's address. Which pipeline construct fits?

options.t: AUTO CDC with KEYS, SEQUENCE BY and STORED AS SCD TYPE 2
AUTO CDC STORED AS SCD TYPE 1, which keeps history by default
options.why: SCD type 1 overwrites; type 2 keeps history.

options.t: A materialized view over the change feed with GROUP BY customer
options.why: That gives one row per customer, not history.

options.t: A streaming table with an append flow, deduplicated later
options.why: Append doesn't apply changes or keep SCD history.

questions.explain: AUTO CDC applies a change feed with keys and a sequencing column, handling out-of-order events, as SCD type 1 (overwrite) or type 2 (history).

questions.q: An expectation must stop the pipeline update when any row has a negative amount. Which action?

options.t: `EXPECT (amount >= 0) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW`
options.why: Drop removes the rows but the update continues.

options.t: `EXPECT (amount >= 0) ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE`
`EXPECT (amount >= 0) ON VIOLATION QUARANTINE`
options.why: Quarantine is a pattern built on top, not an action keyword.

options.t: `EXPECT (amount >= 0)`, the default warn action
options.why: Warn writes the invalid rows and counts them.

questions.explain: Expectation actions: warn (default), drop (ON VIOLATION DROP ROW) and fail (ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE).

questions.q: In a pipeline, which dataset recomputes results to match the source's current state, including updates and deletes in the source?

options.t: A view, which is persisted between updates
options.why: Views aren't persisted.

options.t: A sink
options.why: Sinks write out; they don't recompute.

options.t: A materialized view
A streaming table
options.why: A streaming table processes each appended row once and doesn't recompute.

questions.explain: A materialized view is recomputed as needed, incrementally when possible, so it stays correct when the source updates or deletes; a streaming table assumes an append-only source.

questions.q: A job must run its transformation task only if the ingestion task loaded new rows. Which task type branches on that?

options.t: A For each task over the ingestion task's output
options.why: For each runs a task per element.

options.t: A Run Job task
options.why: That runs another job.

options.t: A dashboard task
options.why: That refreshes a dashboard.

options.t: An If/else condition task

questions.explain: An If/else condition task branches on a boolean expression, for example running transformations only if ingestion added rows.

questions.q: A task sets `dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set(key='rows', value=n)`. How does a later task read it as a parameter?

options.t: `{{tasks.<task_name>.values.rows}}`
`{{task.rows}}`
options.why: That isn't a reference.

options.t: `dbutils.widgets.get('rows')` without any configuration
options.why: A widget reads a parameter the task was given; the task value must be passed in by reference.

options.t: `{{job.parameters.rows}}`
options.why: That reads a job parameter, not a task value.

questions.explain: Task values are referenced as {{tasks.<task_name>.values.<key>}} in a later task's parameters.

questions.q: A For each task runs a notebook for 40 regions. By default, how many iterations run at once?

options.t: All 40, in parallel
options.why: Concurrency defaults to 1.

options.t: One: the Concurrency setting defaults to 1
As many as the cluster has cores, up to the job's limit
options.why: It is a setting of the task, default 1.

options.t: Ten, the workspace limit for nested tasks
options.why: There is no such default.

questions.explain: For each runs one nested task per input element, with a Concurrency setting that defaults to 1; a For each can't nest another For each.

questions.q: Where does Databricks recommend keeping Python functions and their unit tests?

options.t: Inside the notebooks that use them, in a cell at the bottom
options.why: Databricks recommends keeping them outside notebooks.

options.t: In a cluster init script, so they are installed on every node
options.why: Init scripts aren't for code under test.

options.t: In files (not notebooks) in a Git folder, tested with pytest
In a DBFS folder writable by all users
options.why: DBFS libraries are discouraged.

questions.explain: The testing page: keep functions and their tests outside notebooks, in files in a Git folder, with functions that return one predictable result, and run pytest.

questions.q: A unit test must check that a transformation's output DataFrame matches an expected DataFrame. Which PySpark utility is meant for this?

options.t: `df.explain()` compared with the expected plan
options.why: That compares plans, not data.

options.t: `spark.catalog.compare`
options.why: There is no such method.

options.t: `df.show()` compared with a printed string
options.why: Comparing printed output is fragile.

options.t: `pyspark.testing.assertDataFrameEqual`

questions.explain: PySpark's testing module provides assertDataFrameEqual for data and assertSchemaEqual for schemas.

questions.q: What does a Declarative Automation Bundle deploy?

options.t: Resource definitions (jobs, pipelines and others) together with their source files, to a target
Only the job definitions; the notebooks and files they run must be copied to the workspace separately
options.why: A bundle deploys resources with their source files.

options.t: A cluster image with the project's libraries baked in
options.why: Bundles describe resources and files.

options.t: A database migration script for Unity Catalog
options.why: That isn't what bundles are.

questions.explain: A bundle is YAML (databricks.yml plus resource files) describing jobs, pipelines, dashboards and more, deployed with its source files to a target environment.

questions.q: A bundle's dev target uses `mode: development`. What does that mode do to a job's schedule?

options.t: Runs it twice as often for faster feedback
options.why: Development mode pauses schedules.

options.t: Pauses schedules and triggers
Deletes the schedule from the bundle
options.why: It pauses, not deletes.

options.t: Nothing; schedules are unaffected by modes
options.why: Development mode pauses them.

questions.explain: mode: development prefixes resources with [dev <name>], pauses schedules and triggers, allows concurrent runs and disables the deployment lock.

questions.q: A serverless notebook needs an extra Python library. Serverless supports neither init scripts nor compute policies. How is it added?

options.t: Through a compute policy's required libraries
options.why: Serverless doesn't support compute policies.

options.t: By installing PySpark first, then the library
options.why: Never install PySpark on serverless; it stops the session.

options.t: In the notebook's Environment side panel, as a dependency
With a cluster-scoped init script stored in a Unity Catalog volume
options.why: Serverless doesn't support init scripts.

questions.explain: Serverless dependencies go in the Environment side panel, in requirements.txt syntax, with wheels from workspace files or volumes; installing PySpark there breaks the session.

questions.q: For each customer, keep only the latest order. Which approach is deterministic?

options.t: `DISTINCT customer_id, order_id`
options.why: That keeps every distinct order.

options.t: `dropDuplicates(['customer_id'])`, which keeps the row with the newest order for each customer
options.why: Nothing in it picks the newest row.

options.t: `GROUP BY customer_id` with `first(order_id)` and no ordering
options.why: first() without ordering isn't the latest.

options.t: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_ts DESC)` and keep row 1

questions.explain: A ranking window ordered by time per key picks the latest row deterministically; dropDuplicates keeps one row per key without choosing which.

questions.q: A Unity Catalog Python UDF returns the same output for the same input. How do you tell Databricks so?

options.t: Add `DETERMINISTIC` to the function definition
Grant EXECUTE to `account users`
options.why: That is a permission, not a property of the function.

options.t: Set `spark.sql.udf.cache=true` on the warehouse
options.why: No such setting is documented.

options.t: Mark it `STRICT ISOLATION`
options.why: That isolates a UDF's environment; it doesn't declare determinism.

questions.explain: The UC functions page: add DETERMINISTIC to the definition if the function produces the same outputs for the same inputs.
